hints: Think about where each oxide comes from, inside a hot car engine and out in the open air.
Remember petrol contains sulfur impurities while air itself provides both $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ for high temperature reactions.
Link each gas to rainwater, both $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{NO}_2$ dissolve to make strong acids.
walkthrough:
**Check statement 1 - engines**

Think like a detective inside an engine. It is very hot and it burns fuel in air.

Air provides $\text{N}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NO}$ at high temperature, and sulfur impurities in the fuel burn: $$\text{S} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{SO}_2$$ So statement 1 is true.

**Check statement 2 - direct combination**

Direct combination just means element + oxygen. Sulfur burns easily in oxygen to give $\text{SO}_2$.

Nitrogen is much less reactive, but with lightning or very high heat it does combine directly: $$\text{N}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NO}$$ So statement 2 is also true.

**Check statement 3 - acid rain**

Both types of oxide dissolve in cloud water to make acid. Sulfur dioxide makes sulfurous and sulfuric acid.

Reactions include: $$2\text{SO}_2 + \text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$$ and $$4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{HNO}_3$$ So statement 3 is true, and 1, 2 and 3 are all correct.

options.A: Correct, because all three statements are true. Engines make both $\text{NO}_x$ from air and $\text{SO}_2$ from fuel sulfur, both elements combine directly with oxygen, and both oxides form acids ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and $\text{HNO}_3$) in rain.
options.B: Incorrect, this option suggests only 1 and 2 are correct. Students choose this if they forget that nitrogen oxides also cause acid rain, not just sulfur dioxide.
options.C: Incorrect, this option suggests only 2 and 3 are correct. Students choose this if they think sulfur oxides cannot form in engines because air has no sulfur, forgetting about sulfur impurities in petrol and diesel.
options.D: Incorrect, this option suggests only 1 is correct. Students choose this if they think nitrogen is too unreactive to combine directly with oxygen, forgetting that lightning and very high temperatures force $\text{N}_2 + \text{O}_2$ to react.
